stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy receives a Focalin prescription issued four days ago by a properly registered New Hampshire prescriber. The pharmacist verifies the prescription and prescriber. Which conclusion is most defensible?

choices.text: Reject it because all out-of-state Schedule II prescriptions are prohibited.
Apply the five-day contiguous-state narcotic rule because all Schedule II drugs are narcotics.
Dispense under the nonnarcotic Schedule II out-of-state pathway after verification.
Use the 30-day out-of-state Schedule III-through-VI window.
Dispense without verification because New Hampshire is contiguous.

explanation.core_reasoning: Dispense under the nonnarcotic Schedule II out-of-state pathway after verification. By contrast, 'Reject it because all out-of-state Schedule II prescriptions are prohibited.' uses a legal trigger absent from the stem.

choice_analysis.C: The stated facts support this result: Dispense under the nonnarcotic Schedule II out-of-state pathway after verification.
choice_analysis.D: This near-miss uses a different trigger: Use the 30-day out-of-state Schedule III-through-VI window.
choice_analysis.E: This near-miss uses a different trigger: Dispense without verification because New Hampshire is contiguous.

related_facts: dexmethylphenidate (Focalin) is used for attention deficit hyperactivity disorder; it is federal Schedule II and Massachusetts Schedule II.
Massachusetts applies a five-day presentation window and different issuing-state conditions to out-of-state narcotic and nonnarcotic Schedule II prescriptions.
